name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MINERALNUTRITION_MCQ_Q01 - Pioneer of hydroponics technique in 1860

questiontext.text: Who demonstrated for the first time in 1860 that plants could be grown to maturity in a defined nutrient solution in complete absence of soil?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Hydroponics is the technique of growing plants in a soil-free, defined mineral nutrient solution.

Step 2: Historical Fact
In 1860, the prominent German botanist Julius von Sachs demonstrated for the first time that plants could be grown to maturity in a defined nutrient solution without soil.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The scientist who first demonstrated hydroponics in 1860 was Julius von Sachs.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MINERALNUTRITION_MCQ_Q02 - Commercial vegetables produced via hydroponics

questiontext.text: Hydroponics has been successfully employed as a technique for the commercial production of which of the following sets of vegetables?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Beyond laboratory identification of essential elements and deficiency symptoms, hydroponics is used commercially for high-value crops.

Step 2: Application
Hydroponics has been successfully employed for the commercial production of vegetables such as tomato, seedless cucumber, and lettuce.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The commercial hydroponic vegetables are tomato, seedless cucumber, and lettuce.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MINERALNUTRITION_MCQ_Q03 - Quantitative threshold for plant macronutrients

questiontext.text: Macronutrients are generally present in plant tissues in concentrations:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Essential elements are divided into macronutrients and micronutrients based on their quantitative requirements in plant tissues.

Step 2: Quantitative Threshold
Macronutrients are generally present in plant tissues in large amounts, specifically in excess of 10 mmole kg-1 of dry matter, whereas micronutrients are needed in amounts less than 10 mmole kg-1 of dry matter.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Macronutrients are present in excess of 10 mmole kg-1 of dry matter.

answer.text: Less than 10 mmole kg-1 of dry matter
Between 1 and 5 mmole kg-1 of fresh weight
In excess of 10 mmole kg-1 of dry matter

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MINERALNUTRITION_MCQ_Q04 - Identification of essential micronutrients in plants

questiontext.text: Which of the following groups consists exclusively of essential micronutrients (trace elements) for plants?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
There are 17 essential elements for plant growth and metabolism: 9 macronutrients and 8 micronutrients.

Step 2: Classification Check
The eight micronutrients are iron (Fe), manganese (Mn), copper (Cu), molybdenum (Mo), zinc (Zn), boron (B), chlorine (Cl), and nickel (Ni). Calcium, magnesium, sulphur, potassium, and phosphorus are macronutrients, while sodium and silicon are beneficial elements.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The group consisting exclusively of essential micronutrients is iron, manganese, molybdenum, zinc, and nickel.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MINERALNUTRITION_MCQ_Q05 - Beneficial elements required by higher plants

questiontext.text: In addition to the 17 essential elements, which set of elements is classified as beneficial elements required by higher plants?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Apart from the 17 strictly essential macro- and micronutrients, certain elements provide specific benefits to higher plants.

Step 2: Identification
The beneficial elements required by higher plants are sodium, silicon, cobalt, and selenium.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Sodium, silicon, cobalt, and selenium constitute the beneficial elements.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MINERALNUTRITION_MCQ_Q06 - Nitrogen requirement and primary absorbed form

questiontext.text: Which essential nutrient element is required by plants in the greatest amount, and in what form is it mainly absorbed?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Among all mineral nutrients, nitrogen is a major constituent of proteins, nucleic acids, vitamins, and hormones.

Step 2: Quantitative Requirement and Absorption
Nitrogen is the essential nutrient element required by plants in the greatest amount. It is absorbed mainly as NO3-, though some is also taken up as NO2- or NH4+.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The element required in the greatest amount is nitrogen, absorbed mainly as NO3-.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MINERALNUTRITION_MCQ_Q07 - Definition of chlorosis deficiency symptom

questiontext.text: The deficiency symptom characterised by the loss of chlorophyll leading to yellowing in leaves is known as:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Deficiency of essential mineral elements leads to characteristic morphological changes in plants.

Step 2: Symptom Definition
Chlorosis is defined as the loss of chlorophyll leading to yellowing in leaves, caused by the deficiency of N, K, Mg, S, Fe, Mn, Zn, and Mo. By contrast, necrosis refers to the death of tissue, particularly leaf tissue.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Loss of chlorophyll leading to yellowing in leaves is called chlorosis.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MINERALNUTRITION_MCQ_Q08 - Translocation pathway of mineral salts

questiontext.text: Mineral salts are translocated from the roots to other parts of the plant through which tissue and driving force?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Once mineral ions are absorbed by the roots, they must be distributed throughout the plant body.

Step 2: Mechanism
Mineral salts are translocated through the xylem along with the ascending stream of water, which is pulled up through the plant by transpirational pull.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Mineral salts are translocated through xylem via transpirational pull.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MINERALNUTRITION_MCQ_Q09 - Pigment responsible for pink colour of root nodules

questiontext.text: When a root nodule of a common pulse plant is cut open, the central portion appears red or pink due to the presence of:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Symbiotic root nodules of legumes contain specialised biochemical components required for nitrogen fixation.

Step 2: Pigment Identification
The central portion of a cut legume root nodule is red or pink due to the presence of leguminous haemoglobin, or leghaemoglobin, which acts as an oxygen scavenger.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The pink colour of the central portion of legume root nodules is due to leghaemoglobin.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MINERALNUTRITION_MCQ_Q10 - Importance of purified water and salts in hydroponics

questiontext.text: Why is the use of purified water and purified mineral nutrient salts essential in hydroponic studies aimed at determining the essentiality of elements?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Hydroponic experiments test the effect of adding, substituting, removing, or varying the concentration of a single specific element.

Step 2: Experimental Control
Plants require micronutrients in extremely small (trace) amounts, and techniques can detect minerals even at 10-6 g/mL. If unpurified water or impure salts were used, contaminating trace minerals would mask deficiency symptoms and invalidate conclusions about which elements are essential.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Purified water and salts prevent contamination by unknown trace elements that could mask deficiency symptoms.

answer.text: To increase the osmotic potential of the nutrient solution above that of cell sap
To avoid contamination by unknown trace elements that could mask true deficiency symptoms
To prevent the growth of all aerobic bacteria inside the root cortex
To ensure that carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen are absorbed only through roots

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MINERALNUTRITION_MCQ_Q11 - Criteria for essentiality of mineral elements

questiontext.text: Which of the following is NOT one of the three criteria for establishing the essentiality of a mineral element in plants?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Not all elements detected in plant tissues are essential; essentiality is judged by three strict criteria.

Step 2: Criteria Evaluation
The three criteria for essentiality are: (1) the element must be absolutely necessary for supporting normal growth and reproduction (plants do not complete their life cycle or set seeds without it); (2) its requirement must be specific and not replaceable by another element; and (3) it must be directly involved in the metabolism of the plant. Being present in soil at a concentration greater than 10-6 g/mL is not a criterion for essentiality.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Abundance in soil above 10-6 g/mL is not a criterion for essentiality.

answer.text: The element must be absolutely necessary for supporting normal growth and reproduction.
The requirement of the element must be specific and not replaceable by another element.
The element must be present in the soil at a concentration greater than 10-6 g/mL.
The element must be directly involved in the metabolism of the plant.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MINERALNUTRITION_MCQ_Q12 - Non-essential elements accumulated by plants

questiontext.text: More than sixty of the 105 discovered elements are found in different plants, including gold and radioactive strontium. Which statement best explains this observation?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Roots can take up most minerals present in the soil, even at very low concentrations (such as 10-6 g/mL).

Step 2: Interpretation
Some plant species accumulate selenium or gold, and plants near nuclear test sites take up radioactive strontium. However, mere presence or accumulation in plant tissues does not make an element essential; only 17 elements satisfy the three criteria for essentiality.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Many minerals present in soil enter plants through roots, but not all elements found in a plant are essential for its survival.

answer.text: All elements detected inside a plant cell are essential for completing its life cycle.
Gold and radioactive strontium are macronutrients required in excess of 10 mmole kg-1 dry matter.
Plants actively select and absorb only the 17 essential elements from the soil.
Most minerals present in soil can enter plants through roots, even if they are not essential for plant growth and metabolism.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MINERALNUTRITION_MCQ_Q13 - Functional classification of essential elements

questiontext.text: On the basis of diverse functions, essential elements that are components of energy-related chemical compounds in plants are exemplified by:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Essential elements are grouped into four broad functional categories: structural components of biomolecules, components of energy-related compounds, enzyme activators/inhibitors, and regulators of osmotic potential.

Step 2: Category Matching
Magnesium in chlorophyll and phosphorus in ATP are the classic examples of essential elements that form components of energy-related chemical compounds in plants.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Magnesium in chlorophyll and phosphorus in ATP represent components of energy-related chemical compounds.

answer.text: Magnesium in chlorophyll and phosphorus in ATP

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MINERALNUTRITION_MCQ_Q14 - Absorbed forms and roles of phosphorus

questiontext.text: Phosphorus is absorbed by plants from the soil in the form of phosphate ions and is essential because it:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Phosphorus is a macronutrient absorbed from soil as H2PO4- or HPO42-.

Step 2: Functional Role
Phosphorus is a constituent of cell membranes, certain proteins, all nucleic acids and nucleotides, and is required for all phosphorylation reactions.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Phosphorus is a constituent of cell membranes, nucleic acids, nucleotides, and is required for all phosphorylation reactions.

answer.text: Forms the ring structure of chlorophyll and maintains ribosome structure
Is a constituent of cell membranes, nucleic acids, and nucleotides, and is required for all phosphorylation reactions
Is required for the synthesis of auxin and activation of carboxylases
Acts as an oxygen scavenger inside leguminous root nodules

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MINERALNUTRITION_MCQ_Q15 - Role of potassium in plant cells

questiontext.text: Which of the following functions is NOT associated with potassium (K+) in plants?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Potassium is absorbed as K+ and is required in abundant quantities in meristematic tissues, buds, leaves, and root tips.

Step 2: Function Check
Potassium helps maintain an anion-cation balance in cells, is involved in protein synthesis, opening and closing of stomata, activation of enzymes, and maintenance of cell turgidity. Forming calcium pectate in the middle lamella is a function of calcium, not potassium.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Synthesis of the middle lamella as pectate is not a function of potassium.

answer.text: Maintenance of anion-cation balance and turgidity of cells
Synthesis of the middle lamella in the cell wall during cell division

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MINERALNUTRITION_MCQ_Q16 - Functions and tissue accumulation of calcium

questiontext.text: During cell division, which mineral ion is used in the synthesis of the middle lamella as pectate and is also needed during the formation of the mitotic spindle?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Calcium is absorbed from the soil as Ca2+ ions and is required by meristematic and differentiating tissues.

Step 2: Role in Cell Division
During cell division, calcium is used in the synthesis of cell wall, particularly as calcium pectate in the middle lamella, and is also needed during the formation of the mitotic spindle. It accumulates in older leaves.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The mineral ion required for calcium pectate in the middle lamella and mitotic spindle formation is Ca2+.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MINERALNUTRITION_MCQ_Q17 - Sulphur-containing amino acids and coenzymes

questiontext.text: Plants obtain sulphur in the form of sulphate (SO42-). Sulphur is an essential constituent of which pair of amino acids?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Sulphur is a macronutrient absorbed as sulphate (SO42-) and incorporated into specific organic molecules.

Step 2: Biomolecular Presence
Sulphur is present in two amino acids—cysteine and methionine—and is the main constituent of several coenzymes, vitamins (thiamine, biotin, Coenzyme A), and ferredoxin.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The two sulphur-containing amino acids are cysteine and methionine.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MINERALNUTRITION_MCQ_Q18 - Quantitative demand and redox role of iron

questiontext.text: Which micronutrient is required in larger amounts compared to other micronutrients, is reversibly oxidised from +2 to +3 state during electron transfer, and activates catalase?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Iron is obtained by plants in the form of ferric ions (Fe3+).

Step 2: Specific Properties
Iron is required in larger amounts in comparison to other micronutrients. It is an important constituent of electron-transfer proteins like ferredoxin and cytochromes, is reversibly oxidised from Fe2+ to Fe3+ during electron transfer, activates the catalase enzyme, and is essential for chlorophyll formation.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The micronutrient described is iron.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MINERALNUTRITION_MCQ_Q19 - Role of zinc in enzyme activation and auxin synthesis

questiontext.text: Plants obtain zinc as Zn2+ ions. Besides activating carboxylases and alcohol dehydrogenase, zinc is specifically needed in the synthesis of:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Zinc (Zn2+) is a micronutrient involved in enzyme activation and hormone biosynthesis.

Step 2: Specific Function
Zinc activates various enzymes, especially carboxylases (and alcohol dehydrogenase), and is also needed in the synthesis of the plant growth hormone auxin.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Zinc is needed in the synthesis of auxin.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MINERALNUTRITION_MCQ_Q20 - Copper redox property in plant enzymes

questiontext.text: Which micronutrient is absorbed as cupric ions (Cu2+), is associated with enzymes involved in redox reactions, and is reversibly oxidised between +1 and +2 oxidation states?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Certain micronutrients participate in biological redox reactions by undergoing reversible changes in oxidation state.

Step 2: Identification
Copper is absorbed as cupric ions (Cu2+). Like iron, it is associated with certain enzymes involved in redox reactions and is reversibly oxidised from Cu+ to Cu2+.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The micronutrient absorbed as Cu2+ and reversibly oxidised from Cu+ to Cu2+ is copper.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MINERALNUTRITION_MCQ_Q21 - Role of chlorine in water-splitting and ion balance

questiontext.text: Along with Na+ and K+, which anion helps determine solute concentration and anion-cation balance in cells and is also essential for the water-splitting reaction in photosynthesis?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Chlorine is absorbed in the form of the chloride anion (Cl-).

Step 2: Physiological Roles
Along with Na+ and K+, Cl- helps determine solute concentration and the anion-cation balance in cells. It is also essential (along with Mn2+) for the water-splitting reaction in photosynthesis that leads to oxygen evolution.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The anion is chloride (Cl-).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MINERALNUTRITION_MCQ_Q22 - Definition of critical concentration

questiontext.text: In mineral nutrition, the term "critical concentration" refers to:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
When the supply of an essential element becomes limited, plant growth is retarded.

Step 2: Definition
The concentration of an essential element below which plant growth is retarded is termed the critical concentration. The element is said to be deficient when present below this concentration.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Critical concentration is the concentration of an essential element below which plant growth is retarded.

answer.text: The concentration of a micronutrient that reduces dry weight of tissues by 10 per cent
The concentration of an essential element below which plant growth is retarded
The maximum concentration of a macronutrient that a plant can absorb into the apoplast
The threshold concentration of ammonia that becomes non-toxic to root cells

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MINERALNUTRITION_MCQ_Q23 - Deficiency symptoms of immobile elements in young tissues

questiontext.text: Deficiency symptoms tend to appear first in the young tissues when the deficient elements are:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The location where deficiency symptoms first appear depends on the mobility of the element within the plant.

Step 2: Mobility of Structural Elements
Elements such as sulphur and calcium are part of the structural components of the cell and are relatively immobile, so they are not easily released or transported out of mature organs. Consequently, their deficiency symptoms appear first in the young developing tissues.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Deficiency symptoms appear first in young tissues when the elements are relatively immobile, such as sulphur and calcium.

answer.text: Actively mobilised from older leaves, such as nitrogen and potassium
Actively exported to roots, such as magnesium and phosphorus
Relatively immobile and not transported out of mature organs, such as sulphur and calcium
Rapidly volatilised from older leaves, such as chlorine and boron

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MINERALNUTRITION_MCQ_Q24 - Deficiency symptoms appearing first in senescent leaves

questiontext.text: The deficiency symptoms of which set of elements become visible first in the older (senescent) leaves because they are actively mobilised to young developing tissues?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
For actively mobile elements, biomolecules in older leaves are broken down during deficiency, releasing those elements for transport to younger leaves.

Step 2: Identification
Nitrogen, potassium, and magnesium are actively mobilised within plants, so their deficiency symptoms appear first in the senescent (older) leaves.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The elements whose deficiency symptoms appear first in senescent leaves are nitrogen, potassium, and magnesium.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MINERALNUTRITION_MCQ_Q25 - Elements whose deficiency causes leaf necrosis

questiontext.text: Necrosis, or death of tissue particularly in leaves, is caused by the deficiency of which group of elements?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Different deficiency symptoms are associated with specific subsets of essential elements.

Step 2: Symptom Correlation
Necrosis (death of tissue, especially leaf tissue) is caused by the deficiency of Ca, Mg, Cu, and K.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Necrosis is caused by the deficiency of Ca, Mg, Cu, and K.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MINERALNUTRITION_MCQ_Q26 - Mechanism of apoplast uptake and ion flux

questiontext.text: In the first phase of mineral ion absorption by plant cells, ions rapidly enter the apoplast passively through:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Absorption of mineral elements occurs in two phases: an initial rapid passive uptake into the apoplast ('free space' or 'outer space') and a slower active uptake into the symplast ('inner space').

Step 2: Transport Pathway
The passive movement of ions into the apoplast usually occurs through ion-channels, which are trans-membrane proteins functioning as selective pores.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Passive apoplastic ion uptake occurs through ion-channels (trans-membrane proteins functioning as selective pores).

answer.text: Ion-channels, the trans-membrane proteins functioning as selective pores

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MINERALNUTRITION_MCQ_Q27 - Soil as a reservoir of mineral nutrients

questiontext.text: How do the majority of essential mineral nutrients first become available to plant roots in the soil?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Soil serves as the primary reservoir of essential mineral elements for terrestrial plants.

Step 2: Origin of Soil Minerals
Majority of the nutrients essential for plant growth and development become available to roots due to the weathering and breakdown of rocks, which enrich the soil with dissolved ions and inorganic salts.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Mineral nutrients become available in soil through the weathering and breakdown of rocks.

answer.text: Direct absorption of atmospheric gases by root hairs
Synthesis of inorganic elements by root cortical cells
Weathering and breakdown of rocks enriching the soil with dissolved ions and salts
Conversion of organic carbohydrates into mineral salts by mycorrhizae

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MINERALNUTRITION_MCQ_Q28 - Abiotic sources of atmospheric nitrogen oxides

questiontext.text: In nature, which pair of abiotic factors provides sufficient energy to break the strong triple covalent bond of N2 and convert atmospheric nitrogen into nitrogen oxides (NO, NO2, N2O)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Atmospheric nitrogen exists as two nitrogen atoms joined by a very strong triple covalent bond (N≡N), requiring high energy to convert into nitrogen oxides.

Step 2: Natural Abiotic Energy Sources
In nature, lightning and ultraviolet radiation provide enough energy to convert nitrogen to nitrogen oxides (NO, NO2, N2O).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Lightning and ultraviolet radiation are the natural abiotic energy sources for converting N2 to nitrogen oxides.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MINERALNUTRITION_MCQ_Q29 - Nutritional mode of nitrifying soil bacteria

questiontext.text: The nitrifying bacteria Nitrosomonas, Nitrococcus, and Nitrobacter are nutritionally classified as:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
During nitrification, ammonia is oxidised to nitrite by Nitrosomonas and/or Nitrococcus, and nitrite is further oxidised to nitrate by Nitrobacter.

Step 2: Mode of Nutrition
These nitrifying bacteria derive energy from inorganic chemical oxidations and are classified as chemoautotrophs.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Nitrifying bacteria are chemoautotrophs.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MINERALNUTRITION_MCQ_Q30 - Free-living nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria

questiontext.text: Which pair of cyanobacteria consists of free-living nitrogen-fixers?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Biological nitrogen fixation is performed by certain prokaryotes, including free-living bacteria and cyanobacteria.

Step 2: Identification
A number of cyanobacteria, such as Anabaena and Nostoc, are free-living nitrogen-fixers. In contrast, Rhizobium and Frankia fix nitrogen as symbionts, and Pseudomonas and Thiobacillus are denitrifiers.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Anabaena and Nostoc are free-living nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MINERALNUTRITION_MCQ_Q31 - Transamination and main amino-donor amino acid

questiontext.text: During transamination in plants, which amino acid acts as the main donor of the amino group (NH2) to the keto group of a keto acid, catalysed by transaminase?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
After ammonium ions are assimilated into glutamate by reductive amination, other amino acids are synthesised by transamination.

Step 2: Reaction Mechanism
Transamination involves the transfer of an amino group from an amino-donor amino acid to the keto group of a keto acid, catalysed by transaminase. Glutamic acid is the main amino acid from which transfer of the NH2 group takes place.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Glutamic acid is the main amino-donor amino acid in transamination.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MINERALNUTRITION_MCQ_Q32 - Quantitative definition of micronutrient toxicity

questiontext.text: Any mineral ion concentration in plant tissues is considered toxic when it:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Micronutrients have a narrow optimum concentration range: a moderate decrease causes deficiency symptoms, while a moderate increase causes toxicity.

Step 2: Quantitative Criterion
Any mineral ion concentration in tissues that reduces the dry weight of tissues by about 10 per cent is considered toxic. Such critical concentrations vary widely among different micronutrients and plant species.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
A mineral ion concentration is considered toxic when it reduces the dry weight of tissues by about 10 per cent.

answer.text: Exceeds 10 mmole kg-1 of fresh root weight
Reduces chlorophyll content in older leaves by 50 per cent
Completely halts apoplastic water movement through xylem
Reduces the dry weight of tissues by about 10 per cent

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MINERALNUTRITION_MCQ_Q33 - Mechanism of manganese toxicity in plants

questiontext.text: The prominent symptom of manganese toxicity is the appearance of brown spots surrounded by chlorotic veins. Which physiological mechanism explains why excess manganese induces deficiencies of iron, magnesium, and calcium?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Excess of one micronutrient can inhibit the uptake, enzyme binding, or translocation of other essential elements.

Step 2: Mechanism of Manganese Interference
Manganese competes with iron and magnesium for uptake, competes with magnesium for binding with enzymes, and inhibits calcium translocation in the shoot apex. Consequently, what appears as manganese toxicity is largely the induced deficiency symptoms of iron, magnesium, and calcium.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Manganese competes with iron and magnesium for uptake, competes with magnesium for enzyme binding, and inhibits calcium translocation in the shoot apex.

answer.text: Manganese competes with iron and magnesium for uptake, competes with magnesium for enzyme binding, and inhibits calcium translocation in the shoot apex.
Manganese precipitates iron, magnesium, and calcium as insoluble phosphates in the apoplast of root hairs.
Manganese blocks stomatal opening, preventing transpirational pull of iron, magnesium, and calcium.
Manganese oxidises chlorophyll directly while converting Ca2+ into calcium pectate in the phloem.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MINERALNUTRITION_MCQ_Q34 - Identifying deficient elements with overlapping symptoms

questiontext.text: Because the deficiency of any single element can cause multiple symptoms and the same symptom (such as chlorosis) may be caused by several different elements, how can one accurately identify the real deficient mineral element?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Overlapping deficiency symptoms make it impossible to diagnose a nutrient deficiency from a single symptom alone.

Step 2: Diagnostic Procedure
To identify the deficient element, one must study all the symptoms developed across all the various parts of the plant, compare them with available standard tables, and account for the fact that different plants respond differently to the deficiency of the same element.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
One must study all symptoms across all parts of the plant and compare them with available standard tables.

answer.text: By examining only the youngest shoot tip for chlorosis
By studying all symptoms developed across all parts of the plant and comparing them with available standard tables
By assuming that any yellowing in older leaves is exclusively due to iron deficiency
By measuring only the rate of transpiration in the xylem vessels

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MINERALNUTRITION_MCQ_Q35 - Multifunctional role of boron in plants

questiontext.text: A plant exhibits impaired Ca2+ uptake and utilisation, defective pollen germination, and reduced carbohydrate translocation. Deficiency of which element absorbed as BO33- or B4O72- is most likely responsible?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Boron is an essential micronutrient absorbed as BO33- or B4O72-.

Step 2: Physiological Functions
Boron is required for uptake and utilisation of Ca2+, membrane functioning, pollen germination, cell elongation, cell differentiation, and carbohydrate translocation.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The element responsible is boron.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MINERALNUTRITION_MCQ_Q36 - Molybdenum in nitrogenase and nitrate reductase

questiontext.text: Which pair of enzymes involved in nitrogen metabolism both contain molybdenum (absorbed as MoO22-) as an essential component?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Molybdenum is a micronutrient obtained by plants in the form of molybdate ions (MoO22-).

Step 2: Enzyme Association
Molybdenum is a component of several enzymes, specifically nitrogenase (which reduces N2 to NH3) and nitrate reductase (which participates in nitrate reduction), both of which are key enzymes in nitrogen metabolism.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Both nitrogenase and nitrate reductase contain molybdenum.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MINERALNUTRITION_MCQ_Q37 - Experimental evidence for xylem translocation of minerals

questiontext.text: Which pair of experimental evidences substantiates the view that mineral salts are translocated through the xylem?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Long-distance translocation of mineral salts occurs upward along with the transpiration stream in the xylem.

Step 2: Experimental Substantiation
Analysis of xylem sap reveals the presence of mineral salts in it, and the use of radioisotopes of mineral elements further substantiates that they are transported through the xylem.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Analysis of xylem sap and use of radioisotopes of mineral elements substantiate xylem translocation of minerals.

answer.text: Analysis of xylem sap and use of radioisotopes of mineral elements
Hydroponic aeration and root hair curling assays

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MINERALNUTRITION_MCQ_Q38 - Balanced equations for nitrification in soil

questiontext.text: During nitrification in soil, how many moles of O2 are required in total to oxidise 2 moles of NH3 completely into 2 moles of NO3-?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Equations
The two sequential reactions of nitrification are:
(i) 2NH3 + 3O2 → 2NO2- + 2H+ + 2H2O
(ii) 2NO2- + O2 → 2NO3-

Step 2: Stoichiometric Addition
Adding the two steps: 3 moles of O2 are consumed in oxidising 2 moles of NH3 to 2 moles of NO2-, and 1 mole of O2 is consumed in oxidising 2 moles of NO2- to 2 moles of NO3-. Total O2 = 3 + 1 = 4 moles.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
A total of 4 moles of O2 is required to completely oxidise 2 moles of NH3 to 2 moles of NO3-.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MINERALNUTRITION_MCQ_Q39 - Aerobic free-living vs anaerobic symbiotic state of Rhizobium

questiontext.text: Which statement accurately describes the lifestyle and oxygen physiology of Rhizobium and Frankia?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Nitrogenase is highly sensitive to molecular oxygen and requires anaerobic conditions, yet symbiotic nitrogen-fixing bacteria also exist outside the host.

Step 2: Physiological Transition
Both Rhizobium and Frankia are free-living in soil, where they live as aerobes (and nitrogenase is not operational). However, as symbionts inside root nodules during nitrogen-fixing events, they become anaerobic, with leghaemoglobin scavenging oxygen to protect nitrogenase.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Both Rhizobium and Frankia are free-living aerobes in soil (with inactive nitrogenase) and become anaerobic during symbiotic nitrogen fixation.

answer.text: They are obligate anaerobes in soil and become aerobic inside root nodules to generate ATP.
They fix nitrogen actively as free-living aerobes in soil without any protection from oxygen.
They live as aerobes under free-living conditions in soil (where nitrogenase is not operational) and become anaerobic during symbiotic nitrogen fixation.
Rhizobium is strictly symbiotic and cannot survive in soil, whereas Frankia is strictly free-living.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MINERALNUTRITION_MCQ_Q40 - ATP stoichiometry and source in nitrogenase reaction

questiontext.text: In symbiotic nitrogen fixation, how many ATP molecules are required to produce 4 molecules of NH3, and what is the immediate source of this ATP?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Reaction Stoichiometry
The nitrogenase-catalysed reaction is:
N2 + 8e- + 8H+ + 16ATP → 2NH3 + H2 + 16ADP + 16Pi.
This shows that 16 ATP are required for every 2 molecules of NH3 produced (i.e., 8 ATP per NH3).

Step 2: Calculation and Energy Source
To produce 4 molecules of NH3, the ATP required is 4 × 8 = 32 ATP. This energy is obtained from the respiration of the host cells.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Producing 4 molecules of NH3 requires 32 ATP, obtained from the respiration of the host cells.

answer.text: 16 ATP, obtained from light reactions inside the root nodule
8 ATP, obtained from denitrification in the soil
64 ATP, obtained from anaerobic fermentation by bacteroids
32 ATP, obtained from the respiration of the host cells

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MINERALNUTRITION_MCQ_Q41 - Reductive amination reaction and enzyme

questiontext.text: In reductive amination, ammonium ion (NH4+) reacts with α-ketoglutaric acid in the presence of NADPH to form:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Ammonium ions are toxic if accumulated and are rapidly incorporated into amino acids via reductive amination or transamination.

Step 2: Reaction Equation
In reductive amination:
α-ketoglutaric acid + NH4+ + NADPH → glutamate + H2O + NADP,
catalysed by the enzyme glutamate dehydrogenase.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Reductive amination produces glutamate (glutamic acid), H2O, and NADP, catalysed by glutamate dehydrogenase.

answer.text: Glutamate, H2O, and NADP, catalysed by glutamate dehydrogenase
Glutamine and ATP, catalysed by nitrate reductase
Aspartic acid and H2, catalysed by nitrogenase

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MINERALNUTRITION_MCQ_Q42 - Formation and xylem transport of plant amides

questiontext.text: The two most important amides in plants—asparagine and glutamine—are formed from aspartic acid and glutamic acid respectively by:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Amides are structural parts of proteins that carry more nitrogen per molecule than amino acids, making them efficient nitrogen-transport compounds.

Step 2: Chemical Modification and Transport
Asparagine and glutamine are formed from aspartic acid and glutamic acid respectively by the addition of another amino group to each, wherein the hydroxyl part of the acid is replaced by another NH2 radicle. Because they contain more nitrogen than amino acids, they are transported to other parts of the plant via xylem vessels.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
They are formed by replacing the hydroxyl part of the acid with another amino radicle, and are transported via xylem vessels.

answer.text: Removing an amino group and transporting them exclusively through phloem sieve tubes
Replacing the hydroxyl part of the acid with another amino radicle, and they are transported via xylem vessels
Oxidising their carboxyl groups with O2, and they remain stored permanently in root nodules
Replacing a hydrogen atom with a phosphate group, and they are exported as nitrates

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MINERALNUTRITION_MCQ_Q43 - Export of fixed nitrogen as ureides in soyabean

questiontext.text: Along with the transpiration stream, the root nodules of plants such as soyabean export fixed nitrogen primarily in the form of ureides because ureides:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Plants such as soyabean export fixed nitrogen from root nodules through the xylem along with the transpiration stream.

Step 2: Chemical Advantage
Ureides, like amides, have a particularly high nitrogen-to-carbon ratio, allowing efficient transport of fixed nitrogen with minimal carbon expenditure.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Soyabean nodules export fixed nitrogen as ureides because these compounds have a particularly high nitrogen-to-carbon ratio.

answer.text: Are gaseous at physiological pH and diffuse directly into guard cells
Act as oxygen scavengers inside the xylem vessels
Are directly reduced by nitrogenase in the leaves

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MINERALNUTRITION_MCQ_Q44 - Critical evaluation of mineral nutrition statements

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements regarding plant mineral nutrition is TRUE?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluate Each Concept
- Not every mineral element present in a plant cell is needed by the cell (for example, gold or radioactive strontium may be absorbed without being essential).
- Nitrogen is highly mobile in plants, so its deficiency symptoms appear first in older senescent leaves, not young leaves.
- Establishing the essentiality of micronutrients is difficult, not easy, because they are required only in trace quantities and require rigorous purification of water and salts.
- Boron deficiency leads to stout axis (a true statement from the chapter concepts).

Step 2: Final Conclusion
The true statement is that boron deficiency leads to stout axis.

answer.text: Every mineral element that is present in a plant cell is needed by the cell.
Nitrogen as a nutrient element is highly immobile in plants.
It is very easy to establish the essentiality of micronutrients because they are required only in trace quantities.
